source.title: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in LLMs with Whiteout
source.citation: Anna Yoo Jeong Ha et al., 2026
source.authors: Anna Yoo Jeong Ha; Ronik Bhaskar; Hai-Tao Zheng; Ben Y. Zhao

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some table layout and OCR artifacts appear, but they do not prevent identifying the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares gradient-ascent and NPO unlearning baselines on PSI protection and model utility, showing a protection–utility tradeoff. Its recovery-attack experiments, however, are on Whiteout rather than those unlearning baselines, so they do not directly test whether attacks recover knowledge after unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attacks against Whiteout, not against GA or NPO after unlearning. It also reports GA/NPO protection and utility results. Cited claims about attacks on unlearning are not the paper’s own results. Prompt examples and attack instructions are experimental content, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewer.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes Whiteout, an overwriting method for personally sensitive information (PSI). It tests Whiteout against prompt, GCG, 4-bit quantization, relearning and erasure attacks on three open models, which bears on F in a new setting: PSI associations rather than hazardous knowledge. It also measures PSI protection and utility for GA and NPO unlearning, which bears on A's 'keeps general ability' part. It runs no recovery attacks on the unlearned GA/NPO models, so B–E are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Whiteout overwrites a user–PSI association with about 10 camouflage samples, gives 100% PER on seven LLMs while preserving utility and safety, and resists all tested prompt, GCG, quantization, relearning and erasure attacks. GA, NPO and Refusal reach full protection only at heavy utility cost, with no retain set used. The claimed attack vulnerability of unlearning is cited from prior work, not tested here.
record.recipe_differences: Whiteout uses standard supervised fine-tuning on curated camouflage samples to overwrite a specific user–PSI association; it does not use the GA/NPO unlearning objective. The compared GA and NPO implementations are attributed to OpenUnlearning.
record.method_sensitivity: For the reported GA/NPO protection-first settings, utility varies by method and model. Attack outcomes are reported as 0% for each tested attack on all three tested models; paired-prompt order made no difference.
record.problems: The recovery attacks are tested on Whiteout, not on the GA/NPO unlearning baselines; the attacks therefore do not establish whether unlearned knowledge is recoverable. Only three open models are included in Table 10. The GA/NPO utility figures are reported without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the refusal baseline, Whiteout comparison rows, and safety metric from Table 7 because they do not add GA/NPO recovery-attack evidence; omitted the additional GA/NPO utility-first configurations in Appendix Table 16 to keep the record focused on the protection-first unlearning results. All ten attack types reported in Table 10 are represented.

untested.parts: The 'simple attacks don't recover it' part: no attacks are run on the GA/NPO unlearned models. GA/NPO are run without a retain set, so A's methods as usually implemented are not tested.
No activation-direction ablation or blocking-vs-deletion analysis on unlearned models.
No prompting attacks on unlearned models.

Activation steering or ablation attacks on Whiteout, other-language or in-context attacks, and attacks on Whiteout for DeepSeek, Phi-4, GPT-OSS or GPT-4o-mini. Table 10 covers three 3–4B models and 5 PSI pairs only.

missing.what: Utility-first GA/NPO settings: forgetting fails when utility is kept. GA utility-first PER is 0 on Llama and Gemma and 8 on Phi; NPO β=0.1 PER is 33, 0 and 10, with Gemma ARC-E still 0.03. This is the protection–utility tradeoff bearing on A.

Membership inference (Min-K%) after Whiteout: the true PSI's score falls to the mean of the negative samples, while the camouflage PSI's score rises above them. This is evidence of removal rather than hiding for the counter-method.
Token-level probabilities for a protected birthday drop from about 99–100% to 0.14%/0%/0% (month/day/year), and no true component is in the top 5.
Pre-protection leakage baselines for the attack rows (PER before Whiteout 0.1–11.8%).

record.verdict_notes: Whiteout is an overwriting method, not unlearning in the GA sense; it is treated as an F-type counter-method in a PSI setting. Its outputs are fabricated plausible values rather than refusals. The GA/NPO comparators deliberately omit a retain set (authors' stated limitation), which likely exaggerates their utility loss, so the A verdicts are bounded to that configuration. Attack evaluation covers 5 PSI pairs on three small models, and results are reported with no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures PSI protection and general utility for GA and NPO, but does not test recovery attacks on those unlearned models, nor whether they retain utility without degradation.
No small relearning set is applied to a model after GA/NPO unlearning. Relearning is tested only against Whiteout.
No activation-direction ablation is tested, and the paper does not measure whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
Quantization is tested only on Whiteout-protected weights, not on weights after unlearning.
Prompt attacks are tested only on Whiteout-protected models, not after unlearning.
Whiteout is tested against the listed prompt, quantization, relearning and erasure attacks. Other possible counter-methods or attack settings are not tested.
